new_statements.rule_in_words: Babungo is a tone language (eight lexical pitch types) in which stress is explicitly said to be non-significant / to play no role. Phonetically, prominence falls on the nuclear (root) syllable and on higher-toned syllables; when these conflict, a prefix bearing a higher tone than the root takes the stress, but a higher-toned suffix does not (the root keeps it). An alternative catalog reading is 'no word stress according to the source', since the author treats stress as a by-product of tone and root position rather than an independent word-level category.
new_statements.exceptions: A further clause (context truncated in the snippet, apparently where prefix/suffix and root carry the same tone) reads: '.. on the nuclear syllable, neither syllable seems to be more stressed than the other.' Stress can also be used, weakly, for constituent emphasis at sentence level (§1.11.2.1.2: 'Stress may be used for constituent emphasis, but this is a weak form..'; elsewhere 'stress is a weak means of expressing emphasis').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (prefix + nuclear syllable + suffix; examples 38a-g are individual words); sentence-level use of stress/loudness for emphasis is treated separately in §1.11.2. Statement is qualitative (no instrumental data).
new_statements.identity_note: Schaub 1985 describes Babungo (= Vengo, veng1238; Wikipedia/Glottolog alternates Ngo, Nge, Vengoo, Pengo), the language of Babungo village on the Ndop Plain, Northwest Region, Cameroon; no dialect distinction is made in the material seen.
